text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Swedish power company Sydkraft AB will get compensation in the form of nuclear power from state-owned power company Vattenfall's plant Ringhals when the government closes Sydkraft's nuclear power plant Barseback. Early on Monday, the government and two other parties agreed on a plan to phase out nuclear power and according to media reports they will start with one reactor at Barseback before general elections in September 1998 and the second reactor after.

- The reason why merger negotiations between banks Nordbanken and S-E-Banken were broken off could be that the key holding company in the Wallenberg family's financial empire, Investor AB, did not want to be involved in a bank. Speculation has said Investor might buy the state's 59 percent stake in Nordbanken to ensure that the new bank would be controlled by the Wallenbergs. The clan holds 15 percent in S-E-Banken, which has been in the family for a long time.

- Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, said on Monday that the country's financial sector could handle an immediate switch to euro from crowns when Europe's planned Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) starts in 1999. The worst alternative is a long period of uncertainty with two currencies, meaning two costly systems, the Riksbank said.
- An agreement over the closure of Sweden's nuclear power industry ends block politics, uniting the ruling Social Democrats with the Centre party and the Left party.

- If both reactors at power company Sydkraft AB's nuclear power plant Barseback are closed, Sydkraft could theoretically be compensated with imported Danish electricity and domestic energy deriving from oil and coal. But in extremely dry years and problems with Danish imports the electricity supply in southern Sweden could be threatened.

- Shares in banking groups Nordbanken and S-E-Banken dropped on Monday after news that merger negotiations between the two had ended without conclusions. Shares had been inflated by merger speculation. But sector consolidation activity could be even stronger as Swedish banks scramble to improve their positions on a more international market and to use new techniques fully on the domestic market.

- Negotiations to merge S-E-Banken with state-owned Nordbanken lapsed on Monday, leading to a sharp drop in the share price of both banks. The management of both banks agreed that a merger was correct in the long term and desirable but the prevailing political climate made the move impossible. One source said Sweden's powerful Wallenberg family, that owns 15 percent of S-E-Banken, did not want to give up control.

- The Swedish government reached an agreement over the weekend with other parliamentary parties to start the process next year of closing down the country's 12 nuclear reactors. Over half of Sweden's electricity is generated by nuclear power. Details were to be made public on Tuesday. Sydkraft AB, which generates a large part of southern Sweden's electricity, will be offered several forms of compensation.

- Percy Barnevik, chairman of international engineer ABB, has criticised the government plan to dismantle a Swedish nuclear power plant before the September 1998 election as "unfortunate and wrong". He said public safety would be improved more by spending the money on old nuclear plants in Eastern Europe such as Chernobyl and two others that are even nearer Sweden.

- British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, speaking in Stockholm, said Britain's vision of the future European Union is similar to that of Sweden's. He said Britain believes in intergovernmental action in most areas, not integration.
